Q: Obtaining mutable arrays from immutable A:

Is it possible to obtain an array with O(1) read and write access using a read only array?

Yes, using thaw (in O(n) time) or unsafeThawSTArray (in O(1) time, but you must promise not to use the original read-only array ever again).

Is there a wrapper around pure functions that can represent all array operations in a purely functional way?

Yes, see A Persistent Union-Find Data Structure, Conchon and Filliâtre 2007. I don't know of an existing Haskell implementation of this structure.

Q: Why function must be defined with static when compiling A:

Whenever we add a .c file to the list of files to compile, the compiler works with something called translation units which contains that .c file and all the headers that the file includes. This will then get compiled into an object file of some kind (.o in this case) that is then passed on to the linker.

In this case since you typed cc main.c func.c, you will have two such translation units originating from main.c and func.c both. These contain functions that have external linkage, meaning that the compiler/linker will have to expect that function to get called from elsewhere. Because of that, each resulting object file will contain a function call, which may be called from any other source file. This results in a conflict because of that, detected at the linker stage.

If you make it static then the function gets internal linkage, meaning that each translation unit still ends up with a local copy of the function but it is not exposed to other parts of the program. Where one of the functions (the one in func.c) is never called and therefore removed by link-time optimizations.

The easy fix would be to not include func.c in the compilation, since the contents of that file will get included from main anyway.

The correct fix however, is to follow best practices:

  • Never include anything but header (.h) files.
  • Every .c file shall have its corresponding header file with the same name, which it includes.
  • Every header file should have "header guards" (#ifndef MYHEADER_H #define MYHEADER_H ... #endif.)
  • Every public function in the .c file which should be used by other parts of the program should have a function declaration in the header file (along with the documentation of how to use it).
  • Every private function in the .c file not to be used by other parts of the program should be declared static and without a function declaration in the header. (It may still have a function declaration at the top of the .c file though.)

Q: EasyPHP-Devserver-17 dashboard page doesn' launch A:

Same thing happened to me, but the solution is rather simple (when you know it :D)

  1. Close the existing devserver (You may have to kill the system tray process)

  2. Run the Executable "C:\Program Files (x86)\EasyPHP-Devserver-17\run-devserver.exe" as administrador (Right click and select "Run as administrator")

  3. That's it

The shortcut the EasyPHP17 creates on the desktop doesn't run as admin, so if you start the server with the icon the Dashboard doesn't work, but you can also change the shortcut to run the .exe as administrator.

I've check it twice and it should work.

Q: Dealing with colons in paths stored inside a text file A:

Indeed, the problem is that the " characters become a verbatim part of the paths being read and must therefore be removed.

To offer a more concise and better-performing alternative to your own answer; it works irrespective of whether the paths in the file are (possibly selectively) double-quoted:

$read_paths =
  (Get-Content -ReadCount 0 $pathToFile) -notmatch '^\s*(#|$)' -replace '"'

  • For brevity, $pathToFile is passed positionally to Get-Content's -Path parameter; if it contains a literal file path that happens to contain [ or ] characters, you'd have to target the -LiteralPath parameter explicitly (Get-Content -ReadCount 0 -LiteralPath $pathToFile).

  • Using -ReadCount 0 with Get-Content is a performance optimization that reads all lines from the file into an array of strings at once, as a single operation (rather than streaming the lines, one by one), which not only speeds up reading considerably, but secondarily also ensures that an array is returned even if the input file happens to contain just one line (without -ReadCount 0, you'd have to use @(...), the array-subexpression operator to ensure that).

  • Using -notmatch, the negated regular-expression matching operator and -replace, the regular-expression-based string replacement operator on an array as the input (the LHS) ensures that the operation is performed on each element, which is a feature that is common to PowerShell's comparison operators:

    • -notmatch '^\s*(#|$)' filters out any lines that are:

      • empty
      • blank (all-whitespace)
      • start with #, possibly preceded by whitespace.

    • -replace '"' effectively removes all " chars. from each input string (this should be good enough in the case at hand, given that file paths themselves cannot contain " characters on Windows).
